The returned table has one row per selected node only: ids 2, 4, 6 with labels B, D, F and degrees 3, 2, 2." width="100%"} Exports the currently selected nodes, one row per node, as a Polars DataFrame. It is the selection-scoped version of `get_node_df()`, so the usual workflow is to narrow the graph down with one of the `select_nodes...` or traversal methods and then hand the result to Polars for filtering, aggregation, joining, or export to CSV/Parquet. The graph and the selection are not modified. Use this when: - inspecting the attributes of nodes matched by a selection or traversal - computing summary statistics on a subset of nodes - exporting just part of a graph for reporting or further analysis Two details are worth knowing. Attribute columns are built only from the selected nodes, so an attribute that exists elsewhere in the graph but not on any selected node will not appear as a column. And the `degree` column reports each node's degree in the *whole* graph, not in the subgraph induced by the selection. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : DataFrame with the mandatory columns `id`, `label`, and `type` first, followed by the other attributes found on the selected nodes (alphabetically) and `degree` last. Rows are sorted by `id`, and a node lacking an attribute has `None` in that column. If no nodes are selected, the DataFrame has no rows and just the `id`, `label`, `type` and `degree` columns. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Behaves exactly like `get_node_df()` but draws from the current selection rather than the full graph. That means the same column layout (`id`, `label`, `type` first, other attributes in alphabetical order, `degree` last, rows sorted by `id`) and the same `None`-for-missing semantics. If nothing is selected, an empty DataFrame comes back, so remember to run one of the `select_nodes...` methods first. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only nodes in the current selection appear in the DataFrame. Here the two people over 30 are selected; `Cat` is left out, and the `degree` column counts each node's edges in the full graph: ::: {#67860303 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes( [ ("Ann", {"age": 34, "team": "red"}), ("Bob", {"age": 41, "team": "blue"}), ("Cat", {"age": 27, "team": "red"}), ] ) .add_edges([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat")]) .select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes.get("age", 0) > 30) ) graph.get_node_df_ws() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Since the result is an ordinary Polars DataFrame, it can be summarized directly. Here the high-degree hub of a combined star and path graph is the only node selected: ::: {#7b706813 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_star_graph(10) .add_path_graph(5) .select_nodes_by_degree(min_degree=3) ) df = graph.get_node_df_ws() df.select("id", "degree") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
